title: One in, one out
description: For every new thing that enters your home, one similar thing leaves. Your shelves stay level — and so, often, does your spending.

body.heading: How the rule works
paragraphs: Buy a jumper, and a jumper you no longer wear goes to the charity bag. A new book arrives; a finished one is passed to a friend. The rule applies within categories, which keeps it honest — a new kettle does not excuse keeping five mugs you dislike.

The magic is in the pause it creates at the till. "What will this replace?" is a much sharper question than "do I want this?" If nothing at home deserves to leave, the new thing has not earned its place either.

body.heading: Outgoing is not waste
paragraphs: The leaving item is not thrown away by default: sell it, gift it, swap it, donate it. Money recovered from the outgoing item softens the cost of the incoming one, and someone else gets use from a thing that was only gathering dust for you.
Keeping a donation bag by the door makes the habit effortless. When it fills, it goes — no second round of decisions.

body.heading: Where to relax it
paragraphs: Consumables, gifts you receive, and genuine replacements for broken essentials sit outside the rule. It is a guardrail for accumulation, not a law about living. Use it where clutter and spending creep: clothes, books, kitchen gadgets, games.

Families can adapt it kindly, too: the rule works best as a shared household rhythm rather than a weapon in arguments about each other's purchases. Agree the categories together, and let everyone keep one guilt-free shelf of their own.

takeaway: Adopt one-in-one-out for the categories that creep — clothes, books, gadgets — and let every new arrival justify itself against something you already own.
